Start here. This is a map of content, not a container — every note below lives
in its own file and links onward.

## Materials

- [[Rock weathering classes]] — XW through FR, and what each means for founding

- [[Reduced levels and datums]] — RL conventions and the mistakes that follow from getting them wrong
- [[Groundwater observations]] — what a water level in a hole does and does not tell you

## Working with AI

- [[Reverse prompting]] — hand over context, let the agent ask what it is missing
- [[Graph engineering]] — dependency maps, the fake-edge test, diamonds and checkers

## Decisions

- [[Why pile data carries provenance]] — the Field state model in the pile viewer
- [[Socket compliance is indeterminate by default]] — why unknown never reads as pass

## Templates

- [[Template - site inspection note]]
- [[Template - decision]]

# Open in Obsidian

1. Open Obsidian → **Open folder as vault**
2. Choose the folder this file is in (`STS-Second-Brain`)
3. Trust the vault when prompted — the only thing in `.obsidian/` is graph and
   appearance settings, no plugins or scripts

Graph view is on the left ribbon, or `Ctrl+G`. It comes pre-coloured by folder:

| Colour | Folder |
|---|---|
| Violet | the index |
| Blue | standards |
| Green | materials |
| Orange | methods |
| Red | decisions |
| Amber | reference library |
| Grey | templates |

Local graph (`Ctrl+Shift+G` or the note's ⋮ menu) shows what one note connects
to, which is usually more useful than the whole graph once the vault grows.

## Keeping it in step with the web viewer

The Markdown here is the source of truth. After editing, regenerate the web
viewer's index from the repo:

```bash
node scripts/build-vault-index.mjs
```

The repo copy lives at `sts-playground/second-brain/`. If you edit here and
there, they will drift — pick one as the working copy.

## Related

- [[Index]]

notes.title: Socket compliance is indeterminate by default
notes.body:
# Socket compliance is indeterminate by default

**Decision.** When the required socket length is unknown, socket compliance
returns `indeterminate` — never `compliant`.

## Reasoning

Compliance is achieved measured against required. Our inspection reports carry
the achieved length; the requirement lives on the structural drawing, which we
often do not hold. A tool that defaults to pass in that situation manufactures an
engineering conclusion out of an absence of data.

`indeterminate` is a first-class answer with its own colour in the 3D scene,
deliberately not the same orange as a verified socket, so an unassessed pier
cannot read as approved at a glance.

## What it means in practice

On the Carter Street job all 18 inspected piers report as compliance-unknown,
because the report states no required socket. That is the correct reading of the
available information, and it makes the missing document visible.

## Related

- [[Rock socket length]]
- [[AS 2159 piling]]
- [[Why pile data carries provenance]]

notes.title: Why pile data carries provenance
notes.body:
# Why pile data carries provenance

**Decision.** Every engineering value in the pile viewer is a `Field<T>` carrying
value, state, source and confidence, rather than a bare number.

States: `extracted`, `calculated`, `manual`, `inferred`, `verified`,
`conflicting`, `missing`.

## The problem it solves

Once a number is in a spreadsheet it looks like every other number. A toe level
read off a signed report and a toe level someone estimated from a drawing render
identically, and by the time it matters nobody can tell which is which.

## Consequences

- A missing value stays missing all the way to the screen. A pile with no toe
  level has no length — it does not have a length of zero.
- When two sources disagree the field is `conflicting`, both values are kept, and
  the engineer resolves it. Source priority orders them for review; it does not
  pick a winner, because a higher-priority document is only better if it is also
  the current revision, which the tool cannot confirm.
- Piles missing position, levels or diameter are listed as undrawable with the
  blocker named, rather than placed at the origin with a guessed size.

## Cost

More verbose than plain numbers, and every UI component has to render a state.
Accepted — see [[Reduced levels and datums]] for the failure mode this prevents.

## Related

- [[Socket compliance is indeterminate by default]]

# Reference library

A catalogue of the geotechnical reference material held locally, so it can be
found from the notes that use it.

**These are pointers, not copies.** The standards, papers and textbooks are
licensed or copyright material and are not reproduced in this vault — the notes
record what a document covers and where it sits, and the document itself stays
where it is. Anything relied on for a job is read from the source.

Local root: `C:\Users\pored\Downloads\G materials`

## By topic

- [[Library - Australian Standards]] — AS series held locally
- [[Library - RMS and TfNSW specifications]] — roads specs and test methods
- [[Library - Pells papers on Sydney sandstone and shale]] — the local rock-socket literature
- [[Library - plate load testing]] — PLT procedure, spreadsheets and training
- [[Library - salinity and sodic soils]] — western Sydney salinity guidance

will not open. Worth a tidy before this becomes the reference of record.

notes.title: Library - Pells papers on Sydney sandstone and shale
notes.body:
# Library - Pells papers on Sydney sandstone and shale

`G materials/Pells Paper/`. The local literature behind how sockets in Sydney
sandstone and shale are classified and designed — directly relevant to
[[Rock socket length]] and [[Weathered siltstone]].

| Paper | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Pells, Mostyn & Wong (2019) — Classification of sandstones and shales in the Sydney region | The classification scheme used locally to describe Sydney basin rock |
| Pells — The design of socketed piles in rock | Socket design method, side resistance and end bearing |
| Pells — Bored piles socketed into shale and sandstone | Field behaviour of sockets in the local materials |
| Pells — Foundations on sandstone and shale in the Sydney region | Founding practice across the basin |
| Substance and mass properties for the design of engineering structures in the Hawkesbury Sandstone | Intact vs mass properties — the distinction that matters for defect-controlled rock |

## What to take from these

Intact strength and mass behaviour diverge in bedded rock, which is the point
made in [[Rock strength classes]]. A socket in shale that rates medium on hand
specimens can be governed by bedding partings rather than intact strength.

> Copyright papers. Cite them, do not paste them.

# Library - plate load testing

`G materials/Plate Load Testing/`. Procedure, computation spreadsheets and
training for the light and dynamic plate load kit.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `050-Setup Proceedure for PLT Draft 4 Feb 2024.docx/.pdf` | Our setup procedure — draft status, check before relying on it |
| `ax_v80_en.xltm` | Manufacturer computation template |
| `AX01a recommended Loading Stages 6/7.xlsx` | Loading stage schedules |
| `PLT Calculations for AX01a.pdf`, `Calculations.pdf` | Worked computation |
| `Relationship Between Ev2 and Evd.xlsx` | Static-to-dynamic modulus correlation |
| `AX01 Sample Results with GPS.pdf/.xlsm` | Sample output with positions |
| `BedAnlAx01a_engl V40a.pdf` | Equipment manual |
| `PLT Training Presentation.pptx`, `PLT Electronic Menu Structure Training.pptx` | Training |

## Caution

The Ev2/Evd relationship is a correlation, not an identity, and it is
material-dependent. Reporting a dynamic result as if it were a static modulus
without stating the correlation is the same class of error described in
[[DCP testing]].

notes.body:
# Library - reference texts and parameter sources

Where a parameter comes from when it is not measured on the job. Every value
taken from here is a published correlation, not a site measurement, and is
recorded as such — see [[Why pile data carries provenance]].

| Source | Use |
|---|---|
| Look, *Handbook of Geotechnical Investigation and Design Tables* (2014) | First stop for indicative parameters and correlations |
| `Correlations of Soil Properties.pdf` | Correlation compendium |
| `8 Determination of Geotechnical Parameters.pdf` | Parameter selection method |
| Schnaid, *In Situ Testing in Geomechanics* | Interpreting in-situ tests |
| Das, *Principles of Geotechnical Engineering* (8th ed.) | General reference |
| Lambe & Whitman, *Soil Mechanics* | Fundamentals |
| `SPT direct methods for prediction of pile bearing capacity...pdf` | SPT-to-pile-capacity methods |
| `Munsell Color Chart.pdf` | Colour description — pair with [[Soil description order]] |
| `Shallow Bearing Capacity - Various Methods and Settlement Rev 4.xltm` | Our bearing capacity spreadsheet |
| `Earth pressure calculations.xlsx` | Retaining wall pressures |
| `Working Platforms for tracked plant.pdf` | Working platform design for piling rigs |

## The discipline that matters here

A correlation is valid for the material and test it was derived from. Carrying
an SPT-based capacity into a rock socket, or a sand correlation into clay,
produces a confident number with no basis. State the source and the assumed
material whenever one of these is used.

## Related

- [[DCP testing]]
- [[Library - plate load testing]]

notes.title: Rock strength classes
notes.body:
# Rock strength classes

Field estimates of unconfined compressive strength, per
[[AS 1726 soil and rock description]]. Assessed with a geological pick and
hand pressure, and recorded as an estimate — a field class is not a laboratory
UCS result and should never be reported as one.

| Class | Approx. UCS | Field behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| EL — extremely low | < 0.6 MPa | Crumbles under firm hand pressure |
| VL — very low | 0.6–2 MPa | Peels with a knife; deep pick indentation |
| L — low | 2–6 MPa | Pick indents; cannot be peeled |
| M — medium | 6–20 MPa | Shallow pick indentation |
| H — high | 20–60 MPa | Hand specimen breaks with one firm hammer blow |
| VH — very high | 60–200 MPa | Several blows to break |
| EH — extremely high | > 200 MPa | Chips only |

## The judgement to be careful with

Strength varies with moisture and with defect spacing. A tightly bedded siltstone
can rate medium on intact fragments and behave far weaker as a mass because it
parts along bedding. Log the defects as well as the intact strength.

## Related

- [[Rock weathering classes]]
- [[Rock socket length]]

notes.title: Rock weathering classes
notes.body:
# Rock weathering classes

Per [[AS 1726 soil and rock description]], in decreasing order of weathering:

- **RS** — residual soil. Soil texture; original fabric destroyed.
- **XW** — extremely weathered. Has soil strength but rock fabric survives.
- **HW** — highly weathered. Discoloured throughout, strength much reduced.
- **MW** — moderately weathered. Discoloured, partly reduced strength.
- **SW** — slightly weathered. Slight discolouration, strength near fresh.
- **FR** — fresh. No visible weathering.

## Where the founding decision sits

For bored piers, the usual requirement is founding in rock that is at worst
moderately weathered and of a stated minimum strength — weathering class alone
does not carry the requirement. XW material can look convincingly like rock in
the base of a pier and still behave as a stiff soil. Class it honestly and pair
it with a strength assessment; see [[Rock strength classes]].

## Related

- [[Weathered siltstone]]
- [[Bored pier inspection]]

notes.title: Soil description order
notes.body:
# Soil description order

The sequence a soil description is written in, per [[AS 1726 soil and rock description]].

**SOIL NAME: plasticity or particle characteristics, colour, secondary
components, structure, consistency or density, moisture, origin**

Example as logged: `CLAY: high plasticity, pale grey mottled red-orange, trace
fine sand, stiff, moist, residual`

## Why the order is fixed

Logs are read as a column, scanned for change. Putting the governing material
first means the eye catches the boundary. Everything after it is qualification.

## Consistency vs density

Consistency terms (very soft, soft, firm, stiff, very stiff, hard) are for
cohesive soils. Density index terms (very loose, loose, medium dense, dense,
very dense) are for granular soils. Mixing the two — "dense clay" — is a logging
error that will be picked up in review.

## Related

- [[Rock weathering classes]]
- [[Borehole log conventions]]

notes.title: Weathered siltstone
notes.body:
# Weathered siltstone

The material most of our western Sydney bored piers found on. Ashfield Shale and
related Wianamatta Group siltstones, weathered from the surface down.

## Typical profile

Residual high-plasticity silty clay, pale grey mottled red-orange, roughly
0.0–1.2 m thick, over extremely to moderately weathered siltstone. Rockhead is
often gradational rather than a clean surface, which is why proving it needs the
pier base inspected rather than a depth called from a nearby borehole.

*Source: STS report 26/0988, 24-26 Carter Street Lidcombe, 18 piers inspected
27 Jul 2026 — piers founded 1.8–3.3 m below platform with sockets 0.6–2.0 m.*

## What to watch

- Slaking. Exposed siltstone softens quickly once wet, which is the reason
  [[AS 2159 piling]] wants concrete placed promptly.
- The XW/HW boundary is where most disagreements happen. See
  [[Rock weathering classes]].

## Related

- [[Bored pier inspection]]

Exposed siltstone softens quickly once wet, which is the reason AS 2159 piling wants concrete placed promptly. The XW/HW boundary is where most disagreements happen. See Rock weathering classes. Related Bored pier inspection

notes.title: Bored pier inspection
notes.body:
# Bored pier inspection

What gets checked and recorded at the base of a bored pier before concrete.

## On site

1. Confirm the pier reference against the [[Borehole log conventions|structural drawing]] — pier tag, not just position.
2. Record depth to founding level and depth to rockhead, both below the working platform.
3. Describe the founding material: [[Rock weathering classes|weathering]], [[Rock strength classes|strength]], defects.
4. Measure the achieved socket — see [[Rock socket length]].
5. Confirm the base is clean and free of loose or softened material.
6. Note groundwater — see [[Groundwater observations]].
7. Photograph the base with the pier tag visible in frame.

## What the report can and cannot say

It can say the exposed material was competent and consistent with the design
assumption at the time of inspection. It cannot certify the pile. Acceptance
against the design requirement needs the required socket length from the
approved drawing, which the inspection report often does not carry — see
[[Socket compliance is indeterminate by default]].

## The recurring failure

Reporting a depth without the platform level it was measured from. A depth below
ground is not a level, and once the platform is cut or filled the number means
nothing. See [[Reduced levels and datums]].

## Related

- [[AS 2159 piling]]

notes.title: Borehole log conventions
notes.body:
# Borehole log conventions

How our logs are laid out, and the reasons behind the layout.

## Columns

Depth scale, graphic log, material description, sampling and in-situ tests,
water, and remarks. The depth scale runs downward with the description beside
it, so a reader scanning for a boundary tracks one column.

## Description

Per [[Soil description order]] for soil and the weathering plus strength pairing
for rock — [[Rock weathering classes]], [[Rock strength classes]].

## What must appear on every log

- Hole reference, and the method and rig used.
- Surface RL and its datum, or an explicit note that it is assumed. See
  [[Reduced levels and datums]].
- Date drilled and who logged it.
- Groundwater observations with timing — [[Groundwater observations]].
- Where the log was terminated and why: target depth, refusal, or obstruction.

## Related

- [[AS 1726 soil and rock description]]

notes.title: DCP testing
notes.body:
# DCP testing

Dynamic cone penetrometer — 9 kg hammer, 510 mm drop, driving a 20 mm cone.
Blows per 100 mm increment. Quick, cheap, and shallow.

## What it is good for

Consistency and density profiling in the top couple of metres, checking that
founding material is as expected across a footprint, and identifying soft spots
and fill.

## What it is not

It is not a bearing capacity test. Correlations from blow counts to allowable
bearing pressure carry wide scatter, and they are correlations for the material
type assumed. Applying a sand correlation to clay produces a confident number
that is wrong.

## Reporting

Report the blow count profile. If an allowable bearing pressure is given,
state the correlation used, the assumed material and the depth range it applies
over, and flag refusal or possible obstruction rather than reading it as very
dense material.

## Related

- [[AS 2870 residential site classification]]
- [[Groundwater observations]]

notes.title: Graph engineering
notes.body:
# Graph engineering

A way of laying out agent work as a dependency map rather than a list of steps.

- **Node** — one unit of work. One input, one output. The smaller and more
  defined, the more useful.
- **Edge** — a real dependency. It exists only when the second node consumes
  what the first produced.

## The fake-edge test

Write the steps as boxes, draw an arrow between each consecutive pair, then ask
of every arrow: *does data from A actually go into B?* If not, the arrow is an
artefact of the order you typed things in, and the wait it imposes is free time
you are giving away. Anything with no incoming arrow can start immediately.

Most workflows hold two or three fake edges. "Review file A, then review file B"
is the classic — B never reads A's output.

## The diamond

One node fans out to several independent nodes, which all converge on one node
that combines them. The convergence waits for the slowest branch rather than the
sum of all branches.

Two conditions. The parallel nodes must be genuinely independent, and the
convergence must actually need all of them. If it only needs one, the rest are
wasted work.

## Checker nodes

Parallelism removes the natural checkpoints where you would have spotted a bad
result. A branch that returns nothing, or hallucinates, feeds into synthesis
alongside good branches and the final answer is confidently wrong — with the
error diluted enough to be hard to trace.

A checker sits between the parallel layer and the convergence and does no work
of its own. It looks for empty outputs, outputs that contradict each other,
off-topic results, low confidence, and format errors that would break parsing.
Flagged branches are retried or dropped, never merged.

## Static vs dynamic

Static graphs are fixed before the run: fast, predictable, auditable. Dynamic
graphs grow as they run, with nodes deciding what comes next — flexible, but
what actually ran is not what you drew, which makes debugging and auditing
harder. Reach for static first. Never use dynamic where you need to audit
exactly what ran and why, which for engineering work is most of the time.

## Where this already exists in our work

The `geoflow-verify-graph` skill in this repo is a diamond: independent
read-only verifier agents fan out, a barrier collects their reports, findings
are reduced, fixed, and re-verified. The reduce step is the checker.

## Where graphs break

Three failure modes, all worth designing against before you hit them.

**Context collapse.** Fan out to hundreds of nodes and try to feed every raw
output into one synthesis step, and you exhaust the context window before
synthesis begins. Fix: layer the fan-in — group into batches, summarise each
batch, then consolidate the summaries rather than the raw outputs.

**False independence.** Two nodes look independent because neither prompt
mentions the other, but they write to the same file or share a rate-limited
API. That is a hidden edge. Audit for shared *resources*, not just shared data —
a write conflict needs an edge even with no data dependency.

**Silent node failure.** In a chain a failure stops everything, which is
annoying but obvious. In a graph one dead node among two hundred disappears into
a report that looks complete. Fix: the fan-in checks the count it received
against the count it expected and says so when they differ, rather than quietly
synthesising partial data. This is the same principle as
[[Socket compliance is indeterminate by default]] — missing input produces a
stated gap, never a confident answer.

## Loops versus graphs

A loop is one unit of self-improvement: try, measure, adjust, repeat. Its known
failure is Goodhart — it optimises the metric you named and nothing else, so a
bot tuned to close tickets fast closes them fast while satisfaction falls. A
graph mitigates this structurally: several nodes with different jobs check each
other, so no single metric drives the system.

The shift in practice is that you stop writing the agent that does everything
top to bottom and start designing the dependency structure. The agents fill in
the nodes; you own the edges.

## Caution for engineering use

The parallel-then-combine shape is right for review and search. It is wrong for
anything where one branch's finding should change what another branch looks for
— which happens often in ground investigation, where a single unexpected result
should redirect the whole enquiry rather than being averaged in with the rest.

## Related

- [[Reverse prompting]]
- [[Socket compliance is indeterminate by default]] — a checker in a different guise

notes.title: Groundwater observations
notes.body:
# Groundwater observations

A water level in an open hole is an observation at a moment, not a water table.

## What to record

- Depth to water, and the time since the hole was advanced to that depth.
- Whether water was added during drilling.
- Whether the level was still rising when observed.
- Seepage: at what depth, and whether it was a defined horizon.
- "Not encountered" as an explicit statement, because absence of a note is not
  the same as absence of water.

## Why the caveat matters

In low-permeability clay a hole can take days to equilibrate, so a short-term
reading understates the standing level. In fractured rock the reading may reflect
one defect rather than a regional level. Neither is a design groundwater level
without a standpipe and repeat readings.

## Related

- [[Bored pier inspection]]
- [[DCP testing]]

notes.title: Reduced levels and datums
notes.body:
# Reduced levels and datums

RL is height above a datum, increasing upward. Depth is measured downward from a
surface. They are not interchangeable and the confusion between them causes real
errors.

```
depth below platform = platform RL − toe RL
toe RL              = platform RL − depth below platform
```

## Rules we hold to

- Every depth is recorded with the surface it was measured from.
- Every level records its datum — AHD, or a stated site datum, or "assumed".
- An assumed datum is written as assumed. A level on an assumed datum cannot be
  compared with a surveyed one, and a model built on it is dimensionally right
  and absolutely wrong.

## Where it bites

A report that tabulates depths below ground with no platform RL cannot be turned
into a model with true levels. The pile viewer marks the platform level
`inferred` in that case and flags every level derived from it, rather than
quietly assuming zero — see [[Why pile data carries provenance]].

## Related

- [[Borehole log conventions]]

notes.title: Reverse prompting
notes.body:
# Reverse prompting

Instead of writing a prompt, hand over context and let the agent ask what else it
needs. The useful form is a single question:

> Based on what you know about me and my goals, what more could I give you so you
> can help faster and take more off my plate?

Then: *what can you do right now that moves us toward that?*

## Why it works

Not because the model knows things you don't. It works because the model can see
the shape of the gap in what you've given it, and asking forces you to articulate
things you'd otherwise leave tacit. Most bad AI output traces to missing context
rather than weak reasoning, and this closes that gap faster than you guessing what
to include.

## Where it does not

The model cannot ask about a domain it has no purchase on, so in narrow technical
work you still have to seed it. And questions cost your attention — a long
interview that produces a note you could have written in two minutes is a net
loss. Keep interviews short and aimed at knowledge that is genuinely in your head
and nowhere else.

## How it is used here

The Capture mode in the [[Index|second brain]] viewer is this idea made concrete:
pick a note type and it interviews you, then emits a vault-ready Markdown note
with frontmatter, tags and wikilinks. The questions are a fixed bank rather than
an LLM, so it works offline and produces the same structure every time. A live
model asking follow-ups would need an API key and a backend, which the static
worker does not have.

## Related

- [[Template - site inspection note]]

notes.title: Rock socket length
notes.body:
# Rock socket length

The length of pier penetrating competent rock, measured from proved rockhead to
the toe.

```
socket = top-of-bedrock RL − toe RL
```

## Required vs achieved

Two different numbers that get confused constantly.

- **Required** comes from the approved structural drawing or pile schedule. It
  is a design requirement.
- **Achieved** is what was built and measured on site.

A report giving only the achieved socket cannot demonstrate compliance. The tool
handles this by refusing to call it a pass — see
[[Socket compliance is indeterminate by default]].

## Measuring honestly

Rockhead is often gradational in [[Weathered siltstone]], so the socket depends
on where you call the top of competent rock. Record the weathering class at that
level, not just the depth, so the call can be reviewed.

## Related

- [[Bored pier inspection]]
- [[Why pile data carries provenance]]

# CG24-0137-A - Burra Park desktop review, Badgerys Creek

> **Source document:** Core Geotech Pty Ltd, `CG24-0137-A Rev 0.pdf`, held locally in the
> reference library — see [[Reference library]]. This note is a factual index of
> what the report contains and where to look. The report itself is not
> reproduced here; anything relied on for a job is read from the source.

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Report | CG24-0137-A Rev 0 |
| Issued | 2024-02-05 |
| Author | Core Geotech Pty Ltd |
| Client | Development Risk Management Pty Ltd, Suite 7, 265-271 Pennant Hills Road, Thornleigh NSW 2120 (Attention: Nalin De Silva) |
| Site | 1953-2109 Burra Park, Elizabeth Drive, Badgerys Creek NSW - about 344ha total, with the review limited to the Stage 1 (southern) portion of about 172ha south of the proposed M12 motorway |
| Project | Proposed Industrial Development (Burra Park industrial estate) |
| Document type | geotechnical desktop review and data gap analysis |
| Extraction confidence | high |

## Scope

Desktop review of three earlier Douglas Partners reports plus survey and
cut/fill drawings, to summarise known ground conditions for the Stage 1 land and
identify gaps in the existing data. No new fieldwork was undertaken by CG.

## Fieldwork

Not stated in the report.

## Subsurface profile as logged

- Blacktown residual soil landscape over most of the site - clayey soils derived from Wianamatta Group sedimentary rocks, mostly shale
- South Creek landscape along the creeks - alluvial/fluvial soils transported towards creek lines
- Per DP 2022b: depth to top of weathered rock 1.3m to 4.2m below ground level; depth to medium or higher strength rock 8.0m to more than 10m

## Rock

Reported by Douglas Partners (DP 2022b) from eight boreholes (four from 2020 to
6.7-11.0m, four more to 9-10m, both with NMLC/rock coring). Top of weathered
rock 1.3m to 4.2m depth; medium or higher strength rock 8.0m to >10m. CG
cautions that high strength Minchinbury Sandstone layers may occur at the
Bringelly Shale / Ashfield Shale interface even though this is not shown on
geological maps.

## Groundwater

No groundwater information is given in this document.

See [[Groundwater observations]] for what a level in a hole does and does not
tell you.

## Design values as reported

| Stage 1 study area (south of M12, based on Six Map) | about 172 | ha |

| DP 2022b BH1001 (pad level 60.93, ground 66.7, highest pad ground 69.0) | excavation 8.07m; low strength rock 6.9m; medium to high strength rock >8.52m (limit of borehole) | m |
| DP 2022b BH1002 (pad level 68.35, ground 71.3, highest pad ground 73.0) | excavation 4.65m; low strength rock 5.1m; medium to high strength rock 8.0m | m |
| DP 2022b BH1003 (pad level 70.2, ground 74.8, highest pad ground 75.0) | excavation 4.8m; low strength rock 5.4m; medium to high strength rock >9.02m (limit of borehole) | m |
| DP 2022b BH1004 (pad level 64.8, ground 72.5, highest pad ground 66.5) | excavation 1.7m; low strength rock 3.8m; medium to high strength rock >10.02m (limit of borehole) | m |

**These are the report's numbers, not this vault's.** They apply to the site,
loading and construction method described above and carry the report's own
limitations. Re-derive or re-check before using them anywhere else.

## Recommendations

- Add about 10 to 12 test pits targeting deep cut areas in most pads to characterise salinity and sodicity and refine the salinity management plan, combined with rock depth investigation
- Undertake 5 to 6 test pits with a large excavator where cut depth is 4m to 6m, plus 5 to 6 deep boreholes with rock coring where excavation exceeds 6m, to assess excavation characteristics against the current (not superseded) earthworks plan
- Collect additional Atterberg Limit samples from deeper soils, since the existing five tests were all on shallow material and deep excavated soil will form the pads
- Assess CBR for deeper soils to plan earthworks and direct higher strength cut material into road subgrades and building pads
- Determine the extent of uncontrolled fill (drawing on the roughly 400 test pits already carried out on site) since it must be excavated before filling
- Conclusion: no major geotechnical impediments to the proposed industrial development; the data gaps are flagged so the developer can allow for the cost of the identified minor constraints

## Stated limitations

- Desktop review only - conclusions are based entirely on supplied third-party information, which CG has not verified
- Prepared for the exclusive use of Development Risk Management Pty Ltd for the described development
- The reviewed DP reports cover the whole site including the motorway land, whereas this review addresses only the Stage 1 southern portion
- There is doubt about the accuracy and surface level of the DP borehole locations, and the DP work was based on a now superseded earthworks plan
- The extent of the Stage 1 land is not accurately known
- AS2870 site classification from DP 2019 relates to 1-2 storey residential dwellings and is not directly applicable to industrial sites
- Not to be used as part of a project specification without CG review and agreement; must be read in its entirety with the Information Sheets

## Reviewer flags

Desktop review, no CG fieldwork - the 'fieldwork' list is intentionally empty.
Table 2 (DP 2022b borehole summary) extracted cleanly enough to read, but the
column headings for 'Depth to Low Strength Rock' and 'Depth of Medium to High
Strength Rock' should be checked against the PDF because BH1002 and BH1004 show
low strength rock deeper than the stated excavation depth. Reviewed source
documents: Douglas Partners Geotechnical Land Capability Assessment (Ref.
86457.00, R.001.Rev1, 20 November 2019); Rock Depth Investigation (Ref.
86548.17, R.001.Rev0, 9 December 2022); Salinity Investigation and Preliminary
Salinity Management Plan (Ref. 86548.06, R.001.Rev2, 26 September 2022); site
survey; Arcadis cut/fill drawing BUR-AAP-MP-00-SKE-CI-0003 Rev 01. CG's own text
refers to the salinity report inconsistently as DP 2020a in one place and DP
2022a elsewhere. Prepared by Vipul de Silva, reviewed by Raj Singh. Proposal ref
QU23-0481 Rev 0 dated 14 December 2023.

## Standards cited

AS2870-2011 Residential slabs and footings (referenced for the DP site classification), AS 1726-2017 (cited in the attached Information Sheets for soil and rock descriptions)

notes.title: CG25-0318-A - Pump well, Sydney Olympic Park
notes.body:
# CG25-0318-A - Pump well, Sydney Olympic Park

> **Source document:** Core Geotech Pty Ltd, `CG25-0318-A Rev 0.pdf`, held locally in the
> reference library — see [[Reference library]]. This note is a factual index of
> what the report contains and where to look. The report itself is not
> reproduced here; anything relied on for a job is read from the source.

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Report | CG25-0318-A Rev 0 |
| Issued | 2025-05-08 |
| Author | Core Geotech Pty Ltd |
| Client | H & H Consulting Engineers Pty Ltd, Suite 2.01, 828 Pacific Highway, Gordon NSW 2072 |
| Site | Australia Avenue, Sydney Olympic Park NSW (City of Parramatta LGA; near the toe of the batter of the Golf Driving Range Landfill per Sydney Olympic Park Landfills plan, Drawing No. 001-G-G-0221 REV.K dated 5 February 2023) |
| Project | Proposed Pump Well |
| Document type | geotechnical investigation (with preliminary waste classification by others) |
| Extraction confidence | high |

## Scope

Core Geotech investigated a small parcel on Australia Avenue where a pump well
is planned, requiring roughly 3 m of excavation. Work covered a desktop review,
site walkover, two machine boreholes with SPT, laboratory testing, and
development of a ground model with excavation, retention and foundation
parameters. A subconsultant (DRM) prepared a preliminary waste classification
for the spoil.

## Fieldwork

- Field investigation on 15 April 2025 following a BYDA search and on-site services search by a specialist contractor
- 2 machine boreholes (BH01, BH02) by Stratacore Drilling Pty Ltd using a Massenza M12 track-mounted rig with 120 mm solid flight auger; text states depths of 7.6 to 8 m, both logs record termination at 8 m
- SPT at regular intervals in both boreholes; 5 SPTs logged in BH01 and 5 in BH02
- Disturbed/SPT tube samples collected and sent to NATA-accredited laboratories (ALS, Benchmark Geotechnical) under Chain of Custody
- Boreholes backfilled by hand with excavated spoil
- 8 field moisture content tests
- 2 aggressivity suite tests (BH01 2.5–2.95 m, BH02 4.0–4.45 m)
- Site walkover survey; test locations measured from site features to +/- 2 m

## Subsurface profile as logged

- Unit 1 Topsoil – Silty Sandy CLAY, low to medium plasticity, dark grey, fine to medium grained sand, some grass rootlets, moisture > plastic limit; base 0.2 m
- Unit 2 Fill – Gravelly Sandy CLAY/CLAY, low to high plasticity, grey/dark grey/brown, fine to medium grained sand, brick pieces, fine to medium gravel, moisture > plastic limit; base 2.6–2.8 m (assessed as uncontrolled fill)
- Unit 3a Alluvial – CLAY, high plasticity, dark grey, moisture > plastic limit, wet, very soft; base 4.0 m
- Unit 3b Alluvial – CLAY, high plasticity, grey, moisture >= plastic limit, stiff to very stiff; base 5.5–6.0 m
- Unit 4 Residual – CLAY, medium to high plasticity, brown/grey, fine gravel with ironstone and trace fine grained sand, moisture >= plastic limit; base 7.0 to >8.0 m
- Unit 5 Bedrock – SHALE, extremely weathered, fine grained, dark grey/brown, very low to low strength, Class V; encountered in BH02 only
- Strong petroleum odour noted in the BH01 SPT sample from 2.5–2.95 m; slight petroleum odour in the BH02 sample from 2.5–2.95 m

## Rock

Extremely weathered SHALE, Class V, fine grained, dark grey/brown, very low to
low strength, encountered in BH02 only. Table 1 gives the base of the bedrock
unit as >8.0 m; the BH02 log shows shale from roughly 7 m to termination at 8 m
and the waste-classification summary describes weathered shale from 7 m to 8 m.
Final SPT in BH02 recorded 8 blows then +10 double bounce. No rockhead RL is
given as the logs carry no surface RL or datum. BH01 did not reach rock
(residual clay tending to extremely weathered shale at the base of the hole).

## Groundwater

Groundwater was encountered during the investigation on 15 April 2025 at 2.8 m
in BH01 and 4.0 m in BH02, within low permeability alluvial clay. Levels may not
have stabilised over the short observation period and are expected to fluctuate
with rainfall and temperature; no longer-term monitoring was undertaken and no
RLs/AHD levels are reported.

See [[Groundwater observations]] for what a level in a hole does and does not
tell you.

## Design values as reported

| Value | Figure | Unit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Allowable bearing pressure – footings on well-draining compacted granular coarse fill | 100 | kPa |
| Maximum allowable end bearing pressure – piles founded in very stiff alluvial clay, typical founding depth 3 to 4 m below proposed excavation depth | 250 | kPa |
| Maximum shaft adhesion – below 1.0 m from excavation level | 20 | kPa |
| Shoring design, Fill (Gravelly Sandy Clay/Clay) – unit weight | 16 | kN/m3 |
| Shoring design, Fill – effective friction angle | 25 | degrees |
| Shoring design, Fill – Ko | 0.5 | - |
| Shoring design, Fill – Ka | 0.41 | - |
| Shoring design, Alluvium Clay – unit weight | 17 | kN/m3 |
| Shoring design, Alluvium Clay – effective friction angle | 26 | degrees |
| Shoring design, Alluvium Clay – Ko | 0.5 | - |
| Shoring design, Alluvium Clay – Ka | 0.36 | - |
| Unsupported excavation limit – zone of influence of adjacent structures | 30 degree line from foundation level of adjacent structure | - |
| Field moisture content range (8 samples) | 14.6 to 42.8 | % |
| SPT N – BH01 at approx. 1.0 m (alluvial clay) | 5 (3, 2, 3) | blows/300 mm |
| SPT N – BH01 at 2.5–2.95 m (very soft alluvial clay) | 1 (4, 1, 0) | blows/300 mm |
| SPT N – BH01 at approx. 4.0 m | 15 (4, 7, 8) | blows/300 mm |
| SPT N – BH01 at approx. 5.5 m | 19 (6, 8, 11) | blows/300 mm |
| SPT N – BH01 at approx. 7.5 m | 25 (5, 10, 15) | blows/300 mm |
| SPT N – BH02 at approx. 1.0 m | 14 (7, 9, 5) | blows/300 mm |
| SPT N – BH02 at 2.5–2.95 m | 4 (2, 1, 3) | blows/300 mm |
| SPT N – BH02 at approx. 4.0 m | 10 (3, 4, 6) | blows/300 mm |
| SPT N – BH02 at approx. 5.5 m (residual silty clay) | 29 (9, 14, 15) | blows/300 mm |
| SPT – BH02 in extremely weathered shale (approx. 7.5 m) | 8, +10 double bounce | blows |
| Aggressivity BH01 2.5–2.95 m (Clay/Fill) – pH | 6.5 | - |
| Aggressivity BH01 2.5–2.95 m – conductivity | 1050 | uS/cm |
| Aggressivity BH01 2.5–2.95 m – resistivity | 952 | ohm.cm |
| Aggressivity BH01 2.5–2.95 m – chloride | 3040 | ppm |
| Aggressivity BH01 2.5–2.95 m – sulphate SO4 | 230 | ppm |
| Aggressivity BH02 4.0–4.45 m (Clay/Alluvium) – pH | 8.0 | - |
| Aggressivity BH02 4.0–4.45 m – conductivity | 1100 | uS/cm |
| Aggressivity BH02 4.0–4.45 m – resistivity | 909 | ohm.cm |
| Aggressivity BH02 4.0–4.45 m – chloride | 1000 | ppm |
| Aggressivity BH02 4.0–4.45 m – sulphate SO4 | 450 | ppm |
| Exposure classification – concrete piles, AS 2159-2009 Table 6.4.2(C), soil type B | Non-aggressive | - |
| Exposure classification – steel piles, AS 2159-2009 Table 6.5.2(C), soil type B | Moderate | - |
| Preliminary waste classification – fill at BH01 and BH02 to average 3 m bgl (DRM P25.1008-R01, 2 May 2025) | General Solid Waste (non-putrescible) containing Special Waste (asbestos) | - |
| Asbestos detected – BH1 2.5–2.95 m | Friable asbestos, 15 mm fibrous mass | - |
| Asbestos detected – BH2 0.8–1.0 m | Bonded asbestos, 12 mm cement sheet fragment | - |
| Proposed excavation depth for pump well | about 3 | m |

**These are the report's numbers, not this vault's.** They apply to the site,
loading and construction method described above and carry the report's own
limitations. Re-derive or re-check before using them anywhere else.

## Recommendations

- Commission dilapidation surveys of nearby structures, adjoining public infrastructure (footpath, concrete wall) and above/underground services before excavation starts, and have owners confirm the records
- Excavation through the gravelly sandy clay fill and soft alluvial clay can be achieved with conventional earthmoving plant; refer to the current Safe Work Australia Excavation Work Code of Practice
- Keep unsupported excavations outside the zone of influence of adjacent structures (30 degree line from adjacent foundation level)
- Battering to the required depth is judged impractical given uncontrolled fill, services and sign-structure foundations; use a temporary support system such as shoring boxes with steel struts or vertishores with boards, advanced in step with excavation
- Design shoring using the stated unit weights and earth pressure coefficients; increase coefficients or treat inclined backfill as a surcharge where the backfill surface is not horizontal
- Remove shoring in reverse order of installation, with no worker outside the protection of the support system and no removal until the trench is ready for backfill
- Have a competent person repeatedly check excavation faces and shoring for fretting, slipping, slumping or swelling, since soil condition can change quickly
- Found the structure below the very soft alluvial clay (roughly 3 to 4 m depth), or excavate that layer and replace with compacted well-draining granular coarse fill, then design for 100 kPa
- Where higher capacity is needed, use piles founded in very stiff alluvial or residual clay (250 kPa end bearing, 20 kPa shaft adhesion below 1.0 m from excavation level)
- Manage groundwater inflow by conventional sump and pump or gravity drainage; monitor seepage during excavation and test groundwater quality before discharging to stormwater
- Allow for uplift/buoyancy on the pump well from fluctuating groundwater in detailed design; a one-way or non-return valve may be appropriate subject to confirmation
- Select concrete and steel appropriate to the assessed aggressivity (non-aggressive concrete, moderate steel, soil type B)
- Have CG review architectural, civil and structural drawings to confirm the report recommendations are carried into the design
- Clear all footings of debris and softened material and have them inspected and approved by a structural or geotechnical consultant before pouring concrete
- Have temporary and permanent support designs approved by an experienced consultant, and inspect any excavation deeper than 1.0 m
- Seek further advice if conditions differ significantly from those described
- Waste (per DRM): assume the fill contains friable asbestos and use Class 1 licensed asbestos removal contractors with air monitoring during disturbance, stockpiling and load out; re-classify stockpiled soil before offsite disposal including for acid sulphate soils; assess alluvial clays for acid sulphate soils and contamination before any VENM classification; keep truck registers and disposal receipts and use lawfully licensed facilities

## Stated limitations

- Scope of services may have been limited or amended by time, budget, access and site constraints
- The report is for the exclusive use of H & H Consulting Engineers Pty Ltd, for the specific development and purpose described, and may not contain sufficient information for other purposes, developments or sites
- Information is considered accurate only at the date of issue with regard to conditions at that time
- Conclusions rely on interpolation between two boreholes; conditions can vary between test locations and no investigation can reveal all subsurface details and anomalies
- Depths and layer thicknesses in Table 1 apply at the investigation locations and may not represent the whole site
- CG relied on information supplied by the client and their agents and has not verified its accuracy or completeness
- The report should not be used as part of a project specification without CG's review and agreement
- The report must be kept whole and read with the attached Information Sheets and explanatory notes; CG is not responsible for others' interpretations not supported by an express statement in the report
- Groundwater levels are point-in-time readings that may not reflect longer-term levels and can fluctuate seasonally and with construction activity; no long-term monitoring was carried out
- Test locations were measured from site features to an accuracy of +/- 2 m
- Soil and rock descriptions are based on visual and tactile assessment except where field or laboratory tests were carried out
- The waste classification is preliminary only, based on limited data from two boreholes, and a single classification cannot be applied along the line between them given the variability of Sydney Olympic Park fill

## Reviewer flags

Body text and recommendations extracted cleanly; several internal
inconsistencies and extraction issues should be checked against the source PDF.
(1) Section 5 states boreholes were drilled 'to a depth ranging from 7.6 to 8m'
but both logs record termination at 8 m. (2) Table 1 lists the base of the
bedrock unit as >8.0 m for BH02, while the BH02 log shows extremely weathered
shale from roughly 7 m and the DRM summary states alluvium to 7 m then weathered
shale to 8 m; DRM also describes everything below the fill in both holes as
'alluvium' whereas the CG logs identify residual clay from about 5.5 m. (3) The
BH02 4.0-4.45 m sample is reported with FMC 24.1% in Table 2 but 18.8% in the
aggressivity table (Table 3). (4) Neither borehole log records a surface RL or
datum, so no AHD levels exist anywhere in the report - all depths are below
existing surface. (5) Table 3 (aggressivity) has heavily collapsed column
headers in the extracted text; the values were assigned following the printed
header order (EC uS/cm, resistivity ohm.cm, chloride ppm, sulphate ppm) and
should be verified against the Appendix E certificates. (6) Section 7.2 relies
on the Sydney 1:100,000 Sheet 9130 (1983) but reference item 8 cites the Penrith
1:100,000 Sheet 9030 (1991). (7) DRM records the hydrocarbon odour in BH02 at
2.5 m, whereas the CG logs record a strong petroleum odour in BH01 2.5-2.95 m
and only a slight odour in BH02 at the same depth. (8) DRM notes no visual ACM
during drilling, yet laboratory analysis found friable asbestos in BH1 and
bonded asbestos in BH2 - not contradictory, but worth flagging for the
excavation methodology. (9) The 100/250/20 kPa foundation values are stated
without any supporting calculation or derivation from the SPT data. (10) No RL,
invert level or plan dimensions for the pump well are given; architectural
drawings were not available at the time of reporting.

A subconsultant (DRM) prepared a preliminary waste classification for the spoil. Recommendations Commission dilapidation surveys of nearby structures, adjoining public infrastructure (footpath, concrete wall) and above/underground services before excavation starts, and have owners confirm the records Excavation through the gravelly sandy clay fill and soft alluvial clay can be achieved with conventional earthmoving plant; refer to the current Safe Work Australia Excavation Work Code of Practice Keep unsupported excavations outside the zone of influence of adjacent structures (30 degree line from adjacent foundation level) Battering to the required depth is judged impractical given uncontrolled fill, services and sign structure foundations; (2) Table 1 lists the base of the bedrock unit as 8.0 m for BH02, while the BH02 log shows extremely weathered shale from roughly 7 m and the DRM summary states alluvium to 7 m then weathered shale to 8 m; DRM also describes everything below the fill in both holes as 'alluvium' whereas the CG logs identify residual clay from about 5.5 m. > **Source document:** Core Geotech Pty Ltd, `CG25-0354-E Rev 0.pdf`, held locally in the
> reference library — see [[Reference library]]. This note is a factual index of

| Issued | 2025-08-29 |
| Author | Core Geotech Pty Ltd |
| Client | Development Risk Management Pty Ltd (Attention: Nalin de Silva) |
| Site | 221-227 & 289-311 Luddenham Road, Orchard Hills NSW |
| Project | Proposed Alspec Industrial Business Park |
| Document type | groundwater advice (preliminary advice on design groundwater levels) |
| Extraction confidence | high |

## Scope

Short-form advice reviewing CG's earlier supplementary groundwater investigation
and six rounds of monitoring in eight standpipes, to nominate provisional design
groundwater levels for the bioretention basin, Pad 1 basin, Pad 3A and Flood
Storage Basin 2.

## Fieldwork

- Site inspection by a CG Geotechnical Engineer on 28 August 2025 to gauge eight standpipe wells (BH12 to BH19)
- Six rounds of groundwater monitoring between 17 July and 28 August 2025 across four locations: bioretention and storage basin, Pad 1 basin, Pad 3A near the southern boundary, and Flood Storage Basin 2

## Subsurface profile as logged

Not stated in the report.

## Rock

No rock information is given in this document.

## Groundwater

Six monitoring rounds (17/07, 18/07, 01/08, 05/08, 07/08 and 28/08/2025).
Bioretention basin: BH12 ground RL37.72m AHD, standpipe 3.38m, levels RL34.72
(3.0m) to RL35.30 (2.42m); BH13 ground RL37.72m AHD, standpipe 6.13m, levels
RL34.42 (3.3m) to RL35.42 (2.3m). Pad 1 basin: BH14 ground RL39.86m AHD,
standpipe 3.1m, levels RL37.06 (2.8m) to RL38.96 (0.9m); BH15 ground RL39.86m
AHD, standpipe 2m, none encountered on 17/07 then RL38.98 (0.88m) to RL39.48
(0.38m). Pad 3A: BH16 ground RL44.591m AHD, standpipe 3.25m, levels RL41.491
(3.1m) to RL43.311 (1.28m); BH17 ground RL44.591m AHD, standpipe 2m, none
encountered on 17/07 then RL42.591 (2.0m) to RL43.491 (1.1m). Flood Storage
Basin 2: BH18 ground RL42.565m AHD, standpipe 6.41m, levels RL37.465 (5.1m) to
RL40.115 (2.45m); BH19 ground RL42.565m AHD, standpipe 3.5m, none encountered on
the first two rounds then RL41.065 (1.5m) to RL41.965 (0.6m). Substantial
rainfall fell during the monitoring period; several wells recorded water within
about 0.6m of the surface and multiple wells recorded depths under 1.0m.

See [[Groundwater observations]] for what a level in a hole does and does not
tell you.

## Design values as reported

| Value | Figure | Unit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Design groundwater level, Bioretention Basin (BH12/BH13) | at or above RL35.50 (highest observed RL35.42, BH13) | m AHD |
| Design groundwater level, Pad 1 Basin (BH14/BH15) | at or above RL39.50 (maximum recorded RL39.48) | m AHD |
| Design groundwater level, Pad 3A | no further work required - groundwater is below the excavation level | - |
| Design groundwater level, Flood Storage Basin 2 | at or above RL42.00 (maximum recorded RL41.965) | m AHD |
| Bioretention basin / storage basin invert level | RL34.50 | m AHD |
| Pad 1 basin invert level | RL38.50 | m AHD |
| Pad 3A invert level | RL44.50 | m AHD |
| Flood Storage Basin 2 invert level | RL37.57 | m AHD |
| Monitoring period and rounds | 6 rounds over about six weeks, 17 July to 28 August 2025 | - |
| Shallowest groundwater recorded | about 0.6 | m below ground surface |
| Number of standpipe wells monitored | 8 (BH12 to BH19) | - |

**These are the report's numbers, not this vault's.** They apply to the site,
loading and construction method described above and carry the report's own
limitations. Re-derive or re-check before using them anywhere else.

## Recommendations

- Adopt the nominated provisional design groundwater levels for the bioretention basin, Pad 1 basin and Flood Storage Basin 2
- Treat the assessment as preliminary and confirm it with extended monitoring - determination of design groundwater levels ideally rests on 2 to 3 years of data to capture seasonal and climatic variation
- Note that the highest measured levels reflect elevated conditions from recent wet weather and may reasonably be adopted as provisional design values

## Stated limitations

- Monitoring covers only about six weeks, well short of the 2-3 years normally desirable for design groundwater levels
- Assessment is preliminary and subject to confirmation by longer-term monitoring
- Detailed design of detention basins, bioretention basins and uplift-resisting elements such as liners, cut-off walls or alternative systems is outside CG's current engagement
- Prepared for the exclusive use of Development Risk Management Pty Ltd for the described development
- Conclusions are based on interpolation between boreholes; conditions can vary between test locations
- Must be read in its entirety with the attached Information Sheets

## Reviewer flags

Short advice letter (5 pages including Appendix A). Table 1 is column-scrambled
in the extraction but the monitoring dates and RL/depth pairs were recoverable;
a visual check against the PDF is still worthwhile, particularly for BH13 on
7/08/2025 (RL34.27, 3.45m) which drops well below the neighbouring readings.
Date discrepancy: Section 3 attributes the maximum bioretention reading of
RL35.42m AHD to BH13 on 26/08/2025, but the corresponding column in Table 1 is
headed 28/08/2025. Builds on CG25-0354-D Rev 0 dated 11 August 2025; proposal
ref QU25-0294 Rev 1 dated 10 June 2025. Prepared by Raj Singh.

## Standards cited

AS1726-2017 Geotechnical Site Investigation

## Related notes

- [[AS 1726 soil and rock description]]
- [[Groundwater observations]]
- [[Reduced levels and datums]]

Site inspection of stripping and proof rolling over two areas on the northwest

- Inspection by Raj Singh using a water cart and 40 tonne roller; contractor Devcon Pty Ltd; weather fine and sunny on the day and recently

notes.title: CG25-0933-B - Clovelly staircase upgrade
notes.body:
# CG25-0933-B - Clovelly staircase upgrade

> **Source document:** Core Geotech Pty Ltd, `CG25-0933-B Rev 2.pdf`, held locally in the
> reference library — see [[Reference library]]. This note is a factual index of
> what the report contains and where to look. The report itself is not
> reproduced here; anything relied on for a job is read from the source.

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Report | CG25-0933-B Rev 2 |
| Issued | 2025-09-22 |
| Author | Core Geotech Pty Ltd |
| Client | H & H Consulting Engineers Pty Ltd, Suite 2.01, 828 Pacific Highway, Gordon NSW 2072 |
| Site | Public concrete staircase linking Tower Street and Cliffbrook Parade, Clovelly NSW (Randwick City Council LGA) |
| Project | Proposed Staircase Upgrade |
| Document type | geotechnical investigation with AGS landslide risk assessment |
| Extraction confidence | high |

## Scope

CG investigated the ground beneath an existing public stair on a steep coastal
slope so the stair could be demolished and rebuilt. Work covered a walkover,
hand-auger and cored boreholes, laboratory testing, a qualitative landslide risk
assessment to the AGS 2007 guidelines, and foundation and slope-remediation
advice.

## Fieldwork

- BYDA search and specialist on-site services search before drilling
- Site walkover covering landform, adjacent structures and infrastructure
- Field investigation on 29 July, 26 August and 27 August 2025
- BH01 to BH06: 110mm hand auger, refusal at 0.2m to 1.2m, with DCP testing inside selected holes
- BH07 to BH10: hand auger through soil then NMLC coring with portable rock coring equipment, terminated 3.74m to 4.6m; core photographed
- Groundwater observed during and shortly after drilling; holes backfilled by hand with spoil
- Disturbed soil and rock samples sent to NATA accredited laboratories under Chain of Custody

## Subsurface profile as logged

- Unit 1 Topsoil: Silty Gravelly SAND / Silty SAND, fine to medium grained, dark grey, brown, fine to medium gravel, low plasticity fines, moist; base 0.2 - 0.4m
- Unit 2 Fill: Silty Gravelly Sandy CLAY / Silty Sandy CLAY / Silty SAND, low plasticity, fine to medium grained sand, fine to medium gravel, moisture condition < plastic limit; base >0.4 - 2.0m
- Unit 3 'Probable' Aeolian: Silty SAND, fine to medium grained, brown, grey, low plasticity fines, trace sandstone fragments, moist, very loose (BH06 only); base >0.7m
- Unit 4 'Probable' Residual: Silty Sandy CLAY / Silty CLAY / Clayey SAND, low to high plasticity, dark grey mottled yellow, trace ironstone fragments, moisture >= plastic limit, soft to very stiff; base >1.2 - 2.53m
- Unit 5 'Probable' Boulder: SANDSTONE, extremely to highly weathered, fine to medium grained, light brown to yellowish brown, occasional iron oxide staining, low to medium strength (BH10 only); base 3.3m
- Unit 6a Bedrock: SANDSTONE, highly to moderately weathered, fine to medium grained, light brown to yellowish brown, occasional iron oxide staining, medium strength, Class IV (BH07 and BH08 only); base 2.3 - 2.75m
- Unit 6b Bedrock: SANDSTONE, slightly weathered, fine grained, grey, intact core with minor closed joints, medium to high strength, Class III; base >3.74 - >4.17m

## Rock

Hawkesbury Sandstone (Rh). Class IV highly to moderately weathered sandstone in
BH07/BH08 to 2.3-2.75m, over Class III slightly weathered grey sandstone with
minor closed joints. Competent Class III typically 2.0m to 3.0m depth, but about
4.0m at BH10 where extremely weathered sandstone with repeated core loss was
cored (possibly a decomposed boulder). Is50 0.036 to 0.83MPa (very low to medium
strength); estimated UCS 0.61 to 14MPa. Bedding and defects largely horizontal
with minimal clay seams.

## Groundwater

No groundwater encountered. Minor seepage seen in BH09 at about 2m depth at the
time of investigation. Circulating water used in BH07 to BH10 prevented
measurement during diamond drilling. Levels and seepage may fluctuate with
rainfall and temperature.

See [[Groundwater observations]] for what a level in a hole does and does not
tell you.

## Design values as reported

| Value | Figure | Unit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Site slope (from contour survey) | 23 to 25 | degrees |
| Point Load Strength Index Is50 range (sandstone) | 0.036 to 0.83 | MPa |
| Estimated UCS range (sandstone) | 0.61 to 14 | MPa |
| Serviceability end bearing pressure, Class III Hawkesbury Sandstone | 3,000 | kPa |
| Ultimate compressive socket side shear, Class III | 800 | kPa |
| Design Young's modulus, Class III | 350 | MPa |
| Minimum bored pier socket into Class III sandstone | 1.0 | m |
| Electrical conductivity, BH03 0.8-1.0m | 0.051 | mS/cm |
| ECe, BH03 0.8-1.0m (multiplication factor 8) | 0.41 | dS/m |
| pH, BH03 0.8-1.0m | 7.1 | - |
| Salinity exposure classification, BH03 | A1 | - |
| Annual probability, failure of existing stairs | 0.0001 (10^-4), Unlikely | - |
| Annual probability, hillside slope failure | 0.0001 (10^-4), Unlikely | - |
| Annual probability, failure of new stairs | 0.00001 (10^-5), Rare | - |
| Combined risk to life, person most at risk | 8 x 10^-7 | per annum |
| Anticipated excavation depth for new stair | typically less than 0.5 | m below existing ground |

**These are the report's numbers, not this vault's.** They apply to the site,
loading and construction method described above and carry the report's own
limitations. Re-derive or re-check before using them anywhere else.

## Recommendations

- Shallow strip or pad footings are unsuitable on the steep slope; use bored pier foundations socketed at least 1.0m into Class III sandstone
- Design the superstructure with redundancy and lateral bracing so the stair acts as one integrated unit
- Carry out dilapidation surveys of nearby structures and buried services before construction
- Demolish the existing stair with low-vibration methods, remove uncontrolled fill under geotechnical supervision, and leave existing footings in place to avoid creating voids
- Have a geotechnical engineer inspect the exposed ground after stair removal
- Build lined surface drains on both sides of the stair and catch drains at the slope crest; discharge to stable rock or approved stormwater infrastructure
- Apply biodegradable erosion matting (e.g. jute) and establish deep-rooted native vegetation on exposed soil
- Replace the deteriorated timber logs on the slope with an engineered solution
- Remove or stabilise any loose or dislodged sandstone boulders found during the works
- Inspect the stair and slope regularly, maintain vegetation and drains, and repair erosion protection promptly
- CG to review architectural, civil and structural drawings; footings to be inspected and approved before concrete pour; excavations deeper than 1m to be inspected

## Stated limitations

- Prepared for the exclusive use of H & H Consulting Engineers Pty Ltd for the described development only
- Conclusions rely on interpolation between boreholes; conditions can vary between test locations
- Not to be used as part of a project specification without CG review and agreement
- Must be read whole, with the attached Information Sheets; CG not responsible for others' interpretations
- No construction records or design information for the existing stair were available for review
- Design and certification of any temporary working platform for plant is outside CG's geotechnical scope

## Reviewer flags

Narrative text extracted cleanly; the aggressivity and risk-assessment tables
are column-scrambled in the extraction but values were recoverable by matching
header order. Internal inconsistencies to check: the appendix list cites Site
Investigation Plan Drawing No. CG25-0933-3 while Section 6 cites Drawing
CG25-0933-2; Section 11.1 assesses the fill as uncontrolled 'in accordance with
AS2870-2011' (AS3798 is the usual reference for uncontrolled fill); Section 12
describes the aggressivity classification as applying to 'low permeability soils
(type B)'; Section 10 refers to 'Australian Geogrids LR8' where Geoguide LR8 is
meant. Revision history: Rev 0 and Rev 1 approved 10.09.2025, Rev 2 approved
22.09.2025. Author Gopinath Naga, reviewer Raj Singh.

## Standards cited

AS1726-2017 Geotechnical Site Investigation, AS2870-2011 Residential slabs and footings, AS2159-2009 Piling - Design and installation, AS3798-2007 Guidelines on earthworks for commercial and residential developments, AS4133.4.1 (Point Load Strength Index), APHA (conductivity/pH), HB 160-2006 Soils testing (reconfirmed 2016), Australian Geomechanics Society, Landslide Risk Management Concepts and Guidelines 2007 (AGS Vol 42 No 1, March 2007); Australian Geoguide LR8, Pells, Mostyn, Bertuzzi and Wong, Classification of Sandstones and Shales in the Sydney Region: A forty year review, Vol 54 No 2, June 2019, NSW Environment & Heritage eSPADE, Sydney 1:100,000 Geological Series Sheet 9130 (Edition 1) 1983

- [[AS 2159 piling]]
- [[AS 2870 residential site classification]]
- [[Rock socket length]]
- [[Bored pier inspection]]
- [[Rock weathering classes]]
- [[Rock strength classes]]
- [[Weathered siltstone]]
- [[DCP testing]]
- [[Groundwater observations]]
- [[Borehole log conventions]]
- [[Library - salinity and sodic soils]]
- [[Library - Pells papers on Sydney sandstone and shale]]

# CG25-0945-A - Residential subdivision, Calderwood

> **Source document:** Core Geotech Pty Ltd, `CG25-0945-A Rev 0.pdf`, held locally in the
> reference library — see [[Reference library]]. This note is a factual index of
> what the report contains and where to look. The report itself is not
> reproduced here; anything relied on for a job is read from the source.

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Report | CG25-0945-A Rev 0 |
| Issued | 2025-10-06 |
| Author | Core Geotech Pty Ltd |
| Client | Environmental Group Australia Pty Ltd, 36E Fitzroy Street, Marrickville NSW 2204 |
| Site | 128 North Macquarie Road, Calderwood NSW - Lot 100 DP 1251724, approximately 42 hectares, Shellharbour City Council LGA, bounded by North Macquarie Road to the north and the Illawarra Highway to the south, with Macquarie Rivulet running east-west through the centre |
| Project | Proposed Residential Development (staged residential subdivision - Stages 1, 2 and 3 with internal roads, allotments, drainage reserves and utility corridors, following demolition of existing structures) |
| Document type | geotechnical investigation (including preliminary AS 2870 site classification, qualitative slope stability assessment, salinity and erodibility assessment, and preliminary pavement design) |
| Extraction confidence | high |

## Scope

Core Geotech investigated a 42 ha rural property proposed for staged residential
subdivision, covering both sides of Macquarie Rivulet. The work involved a
desktop review of geological and soil landscape mapping, a site walkover, 26
test pits with adjacent DCP testing, and a laboratory programme, leading to a
ground model and advice on earthworks, batters, retention, footings, pavements,
salinity, aggressivity and slope stability.

## Fieldwork

- Fieldwork carried out on 6 and 7 August 2025 (per report body) after a BYDA search and on-site services location search, under full-time direction of a CG Geotechnical Engineer
- 26 test pits (TP01 to TP26) excavated to depths of 1 m to 3 m using a 5-tonne track-mounted excavator with a 450 mm wide bucket; pits backfilled with spoil and compacted by bucket and tracks
- Individual termination depths: TP01 1.0 m, TP02 2.1 m, TP03 3.0 m, TP04 1.7 m, TP05 to TP18 1.0 m each (TP17 1.0 m), TP19 3.0 m, TP20 2.0 m, TP21 to TP26 1.0 m each
- Dynamic Cone Penetrometer (DCP) tests adjacent to the test pits
- Groundwater observations recorded during excavation and shortly after completion
- Disturbed samples collected and sent to NATA-accredited laboratories (ALS, Benchmark Geotechnical) under Chain of Custody
- Laboratory schedule: 4 CBR (AS 1289.6.1.1), 4 PSD (AS 1289.3.6.1), 6 aggressivity soil set (APHA), 7 Atterberg limits and linear shrinkage (AS 1289 3.1.2, 3.2.1, 3.3.1, 3.4.1), 9 ESP/CEC (APHA), 35 EC/pH (APHA), 36 field moisture content (AS 1289.2.1.1)

## Subsurface profile as logged

- Topsoil - Silty CLAY / Silty Sandy CLAY / Silty Gravelly CLAY, medium plasticity, dark grey, trace fine grained sand, fine to medium gravel, moisture >= plastic limit; base 0.2 to 0.4 m (about 0.1 to 0.3 m thick per Section 10.1)
- 'Probable' Alluvium - Silty CLAY / Silty Gravelly CLAY, medium plasticity, red, brown, orange, grey, with fine grained sand, moisture >= plastic limit, firm to very stiff (locally soft); base >1.0 m; encountered in TP05 to TP07, TP11 to TP14, TP21 to TP24 and TP26 (low-lying ground near Macquarie Rivulet)
- 'Probable' Residual - Silty CLAY / Gravelly CLAY, medium to high plasticity, dark brown, grey, with shale boulders, moisture >= plastic limit, stiff to very stiff (becoming hard with depth); base 0.4 to >3.0 m; encountered in TP01 to TP03, TP08 to TP10, TP15 to TP20 and TP25 (northern, western and eastern elevated ground)
- Bedrock - SANDSTONE and interbedded CONGLOMERATE and Sandstone, extremely to highly weathered, fine to medium grained, brown, with cobbles, low to medium strength; base >1.0 to >2.1 m; recorded in TP02, TP04, TP17, TP20 and TP25
- No uncontrolled fill was observed in any test pit
- Test pit surface RLs range from 19.5 m to 36 m (datum shown as 'm' on the logs)

## Rock

Extremely to highly weathered SANDSTONE and interbedded CONGLOMERATE and
Sandstone, fine to medium grained, brown, with cobbles, low to medium strength.
Table 2 gives the bedrock unit as >1.0 m to >2.1 m depth in TP02, TP04, TP17,
TP20 and TP25; Section 10.1 states weathered sandstone or conglomerate was
encountered at depths between about 1.7 m and 2.1 m. The TP04 log shows
sandstone from 1.0 m depth at RL 23.5 (surface RL 24.5), with excavation refusal
and termination at 1.7 m. Depth-to-rock statements are not internally consistent
(see reviewer notes).

## Groundwater

Groundwater was encountered during the investigation in TP04, TP07, TP09, TP19,
TP20, TP24 and TP26 at depths of approximately 0.7 m to 0.9 m below existing
ground surface, with minor seepage and localised inflow consistent with perched
groundwater or shallow saturated horizons. It was not observed in the remaining
test pits, though moisture conditions were generally at or above the plastic
limit. Levels may not have stabilised over the short observation period, are
expected to fluctuate seasonally and to rise near the surface after prolonged
rainfall or flooding of Macquarie Rivulet, and no longer-term monitoring was
carried out. Surface ponding was observed in low-lying paddocks and along access
tracks on both sides of the rivulet.

See [[Groundwater observations]] for what a level in a hole does and does not
tell you.

## Design values as reported

| Site levels - southern portion | approximately RL 33 m AHD to RL 39 m AHD | m AHD |

**These are the report's numbers, not this vault's.** They apply to the site,
loading and construction method described above and carry the report's own
limitations. Re-derive or re-check before using them anywhere else.

## Recommendations

- Adopt Class P for the site as investigated because of abnormal moisture influences; reassess reactivity and differential movement after bulk earthworks and immediately before building pad construction, since fill depth will vary
- Design slabs and footings using sound geotechnical and structural principles accounting for both reactivity and structural loads, and provide the homeowner with CSIRO BTF-18 maintenance guidance
- Excavate residual soils and very low strength shale with conventional plant, with light ripping or hammering in the upper weathered rock; medium strength bedrock will need moderate to heavy ripping, large hydraulic hammers and rock saws or milling heads for footings and trenches
- Require bulk excavation tenderers to make their own assessment of plant, as excavation rates in rock vary with jointing, strength, machinery and operator
- Run a vibration trial at the start of rock excavation and monitor vibration during works near roads and infrastructure
- Proof roll the exposed subgrade under geotechnical observation, undercut any heaving or pumping areas to a firm base and replace with engineered fill; water and re-roll shrinkage-cracked subgrade
- Reuse excavated residual soils and weathered rock as engineered fill where clean, organic-free and no larger than 75 mm, subject to environmental consultant approval for residential land use
- Place engineered fill in 300 mm loose layers to 95% Standard MDD within +/- 2% Standard OMC under Level 1 supervision to AS 3798-2007, with regular density testing documented in a final Geotechnical Compliance Report
- Remove soft, saturated, compressible, organic or unknown-origin material, particularly in the alluvial ground near Macquarie Rivulet, and treat soft subgrade by undercutting, lime/cement stabilisation (dosage by testing to RMS QA Q3051 or equivalent), geogrid or geotextile reinforcement, or surcharge preloading and staged filling
- Overbuild fill batters at least 1 m beyond design geometry and trim back after filling to achieve edge compaction
- Backfill service trenches with engineered fill in 150 mm loose layers using trench rollers, padfoot attachments or rammers, with maximum 50 mm particle size, especially below stormwater pipes
- Use the stated maximum temporary batter slopes for cuts up to 2 m above groundwater, cover exposed clay and bedrock faces with a waterproof membrane, keep surcharge 2.5H clear, avoid near-vertical excavation in heavy rain, and inspect after rainfall over 30 mm in 24 hours or at any sign of instability
- Retain excavations adjacent to structures, boundaries or services with an in-situ wall system where batters cannot be achieved, designed to AS 4678-2002 using the tabulated parameters and allowing for compaction-induced pressures (AS 4678 Figure J5) and hydrostatic pressure unless permanent drainage is installed
- Adopt 100 kPa for high level footings at least 0.8 m deep in Level 1 engineered fill or very stiff natural clay, provided shrink-swell movements can be accommodated; avoid planters, gardens and grassed areas immediately adjacent to buildings on high level footings and extend pavements around the perimeter to reduce differential movement
- Excavate, clean, inspect and pour footings with minimum delay, or protect the base with at least 75 mm of blinding concrete, and prevent ponding in footing excavations
- Adopt a design subgrade CBR of 4% (or 40 MPa short-term modulus) for internal roads and confirm traffic loading before finalising pavement design; inspect the subgrade after preliminary boxing to identify stabilisation requirements
- Blend, treat, or lime/gypsum stabilise soils with ESP over 15% before reuse, and provide surface drainage control, vegetative cover and erosion protection (turfing, geofabric in concentrated flow paths) during construction
- Maintain surface drainage, minimise uncontrolled fill and protect exposed soils with turf or erosion matting to manage shallow slumping and rutting in the soft near-surface zones
- Manage ongoing erosion and shallow bank instability along Macquarie Rivulet through surface drainage, vegetation maintenance and setback of engineered fill and structures from the top of bank
- Install temporary surface drainage (interceptor drains, sump pumping) where seepage or ponding occurs and incorporate permanent subsoil drainage in detailed design; provide subsoil drains around pavement perimeters with inverts at least 200 mm below subgrade
- Install a network of roughly 6 to 8 standpipe piezometers and monitor groundwater seasonally to confirm design levels for pavements, building platforms and retaining wall drainage
- Carry out a detailed geotechnical investigation at final design levels before detailed design of retaining walls and road pavements
- Inspect any excavation deeper than 1.5 m, review structural drawings, and re-engage the geotechnical engineer if conditions or the design change significantly

## Stated limitations

- Scope of services may have been limited or amended by time, budget, access and site constraints
- The report is for the exclusive use of Environmental Group Australia Pty Ltd for the specific development and purpose described and may not contain sufficient information for other purposes, developments or sites
- Information is considered accurate only at the date of issue with regard to conditions at that time
- Conclusions rely on interpolation between test pits and conditions can vary between test locations
- Depths and layer thicknesses in Table 2 apply at the investigation locations and may not represent the whole site
- CG relied on information provided by the client and their agents and has not verified its accuracy or completeness
- The report should not be used as part of a project specification without CG's review and agreement, being advice and opinion rather than construction instructions
- The report must be kept whole and read with the attached Information Sheets and explanatory notes
- Groundwater levels may not have stabilised over the short observation period and fluctuate with rainfall, temperature and other factors; no longer-term monitoring was carried out
- The AS 2870 site classification is preliminary and must be reassessed after earthworks and before building pad construction
- Pavement designs are preliminary; traffic loadings require confirmation by the client and final material and compaction specifications must be set by the pavement designer
- Only ESP testing was undertaken to assess dispersive potential (no Emerson or dispersion testing)
- Suitability of the site remains contingent on implementing the recommended earthworks, drainage, foundation and groundwater control measures, and CG accepts no responsibility for changed site conditions, design modifications or construction practices outside the scope of the assessment without further review
- Site-specific advice from an experienced geotechnical engineer is required for permanent slope batters

## Reviewer flags

Report body extracted cleanly and the parameter tables are legible; the test pit
logs are not. Points to verify against the source PDF: (1) Fieldwork date
conflict - the body states 6 and 7 August 2025, but all 26 test pit log headers
read 'DATE STARTED 6/7/25 COMPLETED 6/7/25', which reads as 6 July 2025 in
Australian format. The ISO date given here is the report issue date (6 October
2025), which is unambiguous. (2) Depth to rock is inconsistent: Table 2 lists
bedrock in TP02, TP04, TP17, TP20 and TP25 and Section 10.1 puts it at about 1.7
m to 2.1 m, yet the TP17 and TP25 logs terminate at 1.0 m and the TP04 log shows
sandstone from 1.0 m (RL 23.5) with termination at 1.7 m. Rockhead depths should
be re-read from the original logs. (3) Section 8.1 gives a plasticity index
range of 5.5% to 62%, but the minimum PI in Table 3 is 11% - 5.5% is the minimum
linear shrinkage, so the PI lower bound appears to be a transcription slip. (4)
Table 1 lists 7 Atterberg/linear shrinkage tests while Table 3 reports only 6
sets of LL/PI/LS results. (5) Section 8.6 and Section 9.1 refer to 35 EC/pH
samples, but the extracted Table 8 contains only 16 unique rows plus duplicate
TP01 (0.3-0.5) and TP02 (0.8-1.0) rows repeated at the foot of the table - the
full table may not have carried through the extraction. (6) The test pit logs
are column-collapsed in the extracted text: DCP entries appear as isolated 'DCP
= 1' / 'DCP = 2' markers with loose blow-count digits floating beside the strata
descriptions, so per-depth DCP profiles and the water-level symbols cannot be
reconstructed reliably. Only the summary statement of 1 to 2 blows per 100 mm in
the upper 0.8 m and the 19 'NONE ENCOUNTERED' water annotations can be relied
on. (7) Section 7.2 cites the Wollongong 1:250,000 Sheet SI 56-9 Second Edition
1966, while reference item 8 cites the Wollongong - Port Hacking 1:100,000 Sheet
9029-9129 (Edition 1) 1985. (8) Section 10.2 refers to 'Australian Geogrids LR8'
where the appendix list and AGS publication name is Australian Geoguide LR8. (9)
Section 8.3 concludes the tested soils are 'silty clays of low plasticity' and
suitable for engineered fill, which sits awkwardly against the LL up to 84%, PI
up to 62% and the H1-H2 reactivity assessment elsewhere in the report. (10) No
allowable bearing pressure is given for footings founded directly on the
weathered sandstone or conglomerate, and no pile capacities are provided despite
deep foundations being in the stated scope. (11) Table 1 lists 36 FMC tests;
Section 8.1 accounts for 34 soil plus 2 sandstone samples, but Table 3 lists 39
rows - the count should be checked. (12) A design CBR of 4% is adopted although
all four measured CBR values were 8% to 20%; this is conservative but the report
does not state the basis for the reduction.

## Standards cited

AS 1726:2017, AS 2870-2011, AS 2159-2009, AS 3798:2007, AS 4678-2002, AS 1289.2.1.1, AS 1289.3.1.2, AS 1289.3.2.1, AS 1289.3.3.1, AS 1289.3.4.1, AS 1289.3.6.1, AS 1289.5.1.1, AS 1289.6.1.1, Austroads Guide to Pavement Technology Part 2: Pavement Structural Design 2017, TfNSW QA Specification 3051, RMS QA Q3051, AGS Practice Note Guidelines for Landslide Risk Management 2007 (AGS 2007a-c) and Australian Geoguide LR8, CSIRO Building Technology File 18 (BTF-18), WSROC Salinity Code of Practice, NSW Work Health and Safety Code of Practice - Excavation Work
